name: Palletism
tagline: Taste packs of AI images, each with the prompt, palette, and guide, readable over MCP
description:
Palletism is a curated gallery of AI-generated images grouped into taste packs. The homepage says each pack holds the exact prompts, colors, and fonts behind the images, and that an agent can read a pack's palette, fonts, prompts, and rules over MCP. The FAQ says every public pack is free to browse, including prompts, palette, guide, and web-size images, and that a free account gives an agent 200 MCP calls a day with no card. Hobby is marked coming soon. The pricing page says it is planned to add exclusive packs, full-resolution images, whole-pack export, and 3,000 MCP requests a day, and that no payments are collected yet.

The terms, last updated November 9, 2026, call the MCP server read-only and say Palletism is not an image generator. They allow the images, prompts, and guides in your own projects, and they forbid republishing or reselling the catalog, using it to train models, and relying on it for client work without emailing first. They also say Palletism does not promise ownership or copyright in any image or prompt. The connect flow in the site script uses https://palletism.art/mcp with a bearer key. A named image license was not on the pages.
install: claude mcp add --transport http palletism https://palletism.art/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer KEY"
pricing_detail: Public packs, guides, prompts, and web-size images (up to 1200px) are free. A free account includes 200 counted MCP calls a day. Hobby is listed as coming soon, with 3,000 MCP requests a day, exclusive packs, and full-resolution export. The pricing page says no payments are collected and shows no Hobby price.
agent_guidance:
Browse a pack in the browser and copy its prompt and hex palette when you do not need an account. For an agent, sign in, create a key, and connect https://palletism.art/mcp. The terms count tools/call and prompts/get against the 200-call daily limit.

Use the images and prompts in the user's own project. Do not republish the catalog, resell it, or use it as training data. The terms say to email Palletism before client work, and they do not grant ownership of an image or prompt. A pack count was not on the pages.
why_it_matters: It keeps a whole look, prompt, palette, and guide together, and an agent can read that pack over MCP on the free tier.
tier_reason: The free catalog, the 200-call MCP limit, and the November 9 terms are explicit. Hobby is not for sale, and the image terms are a custom grant rather than a named license.
notable_for: taste packs with prompts, palettes, and guides
evidence: Checked https://palletism.art/, /pricing, and /terms on 2026-11-12. All three returned HTTP 200. The FAQ and pricing page state the free tier and the unpriced Hobby plan. The terms are dated November 9, 2026 and state the usage limits. The site script sets the MCP URL to https://palletism.art/mcp; a GET returned HTTP 405. A pack count and a named image license were not on those pages. Source tweet: https://x.com/adityawaslost/status/2120764025348784426.

name: Layro
tagline: React component marketplace that coding agents search and install over MCP
description:
Layro is a React component marketplace. The homepage says Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and any other MCP client can search and install reviewed components, and that the files land in the repo as code you own. The MCP docs name the server https://mcp.layro.dev and the tools search_components, install_plan, submit_component, and my_stats. The homepage also says each component is a shadcn-compatible registry item, and that installing with the CLI needs no account.

The FAQ says to run npx layro-cli init --yes once in a React TypeScript project with Tailwind CSS, then copy the install command from a component page. The CLI writes source into components/layro/. Publishing needs a GitHub account and can use npx layro-cli publish. The licences page, marked draft and last changed November 3, 2026, says each component keeps its author's copyright and carries one of MIT, Apache-2.0, ISC, or BSD-3-Clause, sometimes with a Commons Clause on an indexed library. Browsing, copying, and installing are free with no account, and publishing is free with GitHub. A component count was not on the pages.
install: claude mcp add --transport http layro https://mcp.layro.dev
pricing_detail: Browsing, copying, and installing components is free and needs no account. Publishing is free and needs a GitHub account. No paid plan was on the pages.
agent_guidance:
Connect the MCP server with claude mcp add --transport http layro https://mcp.layro.dev, or run npx layro-cli mcp --client claude. The docs say the first call opens a browser to sign in with GitHub. Installing a component into a project does not need an account: npx layro-cli init --yes, then the command on the component page.

Read the licence on that component's page before you ship it. The marketplace accepts MIT, Apache-2.0, ISC, and BSD-3-Clause, and some indexed libraries add a Commons Clause. The FAQ says component code comes from third parties. Tailwind is required, and the pages do not name the major version.
why_it_matters: An agent can search a reviewed React catalog and install the source over MCP, with the licence stated per component.
tier_reason: The MCP URL, the free install path, and the accepted licences are written down. The licences page is marked draft, licences vary by component, and no catalog size was on the pages.
notable_for: free to browse and install, no account
MIT, Apache-2.0, ISC, or BSD-3-Clause per component

name: CUI
tagline: Immediate-mode C UI library, about 210 components, MIT, about 250 KB for an app
description:
CUI is an immediate-mode UI library in C99. The site meta description says about 210 native UI components, compiled to machine code with no browser or runtime inside, for Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web, and that a complete app is about 250 KB. The README repeats about 210 components, no dependencies, and the MIT license. It says you describe the screen with function calls every frame, and CUI lays it out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws with OpenGL or its own software renderer, including in a browser through WebAssembly.

The README's component groups name buttons, text fields, selects, date and color pickers, tables, a data grid, charts, a code editor, docking, and chat, among others. It says most components work from the keyboard and that some still need a pointer, including the rating, swipe actions, and the reorderable list. The GitHub repository description says about 150 components, with spring motion and full keyboard support. The README instead puts spring animation on the canvas API for your own controls, and it says the keyboard does not reach everything. GitHub API on 2026-11-12 reported the MIT license, 941 stars, and a push the same day. Install is CMake FetchContent at tag v1.4.0, or cui.h and cui.c from a release.
agent_guidance:
Use it for a C or C++ desktop tool that should draw its own controls and stay small. The README's CMake example pins GIT_TAG v1.4.0. There is no npm package. The catalog has no C framework value, so this record's framework facet is unknown rather than a web framework.

The site and the README both say about 210 components. The GitHub description says about 150. Treat both as the authors' own rounded figures, not an enumerated count. The README says most components have keyboard keys and lists parts that still need a pointer. It is not a claim of full keyboard support.
why_it_matters: It is a large MIT component set for C that draws its own UI and can run the same code in a native window or in WebAssembly.
tier_reason: MIT, a live component site, a README with install steps, and a push on 2026-11-12. The site says about 210 components and the repository description says about 150.
notable_for: about 210 components on the site and in the README
C99, OpenGL or a software renderer, WebAssembly
evidence: Checked https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/ on 2026-11-12. HTTP 200. The title and meta description say about 210 components and about 250 KB. Checked the GitHub API and the raw README for yappologistic/CUI the same day. The API description says about 150 components, with spring motion and full keyboard support, license MIT, 941 stars, pushed 2026-11-12. The README says about 210, documents keyboard exceptions, and shows the CMake install at v1.4.0. Source tweet: https://x.com/Yappologistic/status/2118571260284399795.

name: Obel Mono
tagline: Free SIL OFL monospace for terminals and editors, with a variant that masks API keys
description:
Obel Mono is a free monospace from Typographic Systems. The page calls it a variable monospace, weights 100 to 900, Roman and Italic, version 1.003, under SIL OFL 1.1. The download section says it is free for anything you make, and the zip contains Obel Mono and Obel Mono Masked as Roman and Italic, in TTF and WOFF2, plus static TTF, OTF, and a variable TTF. The file tree lists OFL.txt.

Obel Mono Masked is the same family with feature ss01. The page says it recognizes 205 key prefixes from 82 issuers, and that keys show as dots on screen while the file and the clipboard keep every character. A source repository was not linked on the page.
pricing_detail: Free under SIL OFL 1.1. The download section says "Free, for anything you make." No price was on the page.
agent_guidance:
Download ObelMono-1.003.zip from the page. Use Obel Mono for code. Use Obel Mono Masked, feature ss01, when a screen should hide API keys. The page says the file and the clipboard still hold the real characters, so masking is a display feature, not a security boundary.

The license on the page is SIL OFL 1.1. There is no package install and no repository link on the page. Weights run from 100 to 900, Roman and Italic, and the zip also has static and variable files.
why_it_matters: It is a free OFL monospace with a built-in way to hide recognized API keys on screen.
tier_reason: The page states the license, version 1.003, the file formats, and the 205-prefix masking behavior. No source repository was linked.
notable_for: Obel Mono Masked hides 205 key prefixes from 82 issuers
evidence: Checked https://typographic.systems/obel-mono on 2026-11-12. HTTP 200. name: fontzz

description:
fontzz is a set of original type families by Hassan and Youssef. The homepage meta description says thirty-six original type families, every weight from 100 to 900, free under the SIL Open Font License. The HTML body text is only the word fontzz. The page script names the thirty-six families: Halden, Rondel, Tessera, Alder, Mallow, Strata, Plaza, Vesper, Ledger, Folio, Opaline, Signal, Tally, Topsy, Tempo, Pebble, Orbit, Cleft, Beacon, Brioche, Diode, Aurelia, Marquee, Anvil, Gravure, Frontier, Quill, Rewind, Spire, Vector, Vellum, Lustre, Hearth, Cove, Fathom, and Meridian. The same script says each family is free for personal and commercial use under SIL OFL 1.1, and that the license is embedded in the font file.

The GitHub README says the families are drawn entirely in code, with a Python generator, three masters, and no font editor involved, then a variable font, nine static weights, and 285 characters per family. Luffixos/fontzz redirects to Nutlope/fontzz. The LICENSE file is SIL Open Font License 1.1, and its copyright line still names https://github.com/Luffixos/fontzz. GitHub API on 2026-11-12 reported the repository Nutlope/fontzz, 78 stars, a push on 2026-11-02, and license field NOASSERTION. The README does not name an MCP server.
pricing_detail: Free under the SIL Open Font License. The meta description and the repository LICENSE file both say so. No price was stated.

Do not scrape the website for specimens. Its HTML body is the word fontzz. Use the repository https://github.com/Nutlope/fontzz, whose LICENSE file is SIL OFL 1.1, or the zip links the site script builds. Luffixos/fontzz redirects there.

The README says each family has a variable font, nine static weights from 100 to 900, and 285 characters. It also says a Python generator draws the glyphs and that no font editor is involved. The GitHub API license field was NOASSERTION. The LICENSE file text is the source for the OFL claim. The README does not name a model.

name: Stageshow
tagline: Benji Taylor's MIT skill for faux product UI, stills, and cursor demos in React
description:

SKILL.md says the skill builds faux product UI as a still or an animated demo with a cursor, in React and plain CSS, and that its version is 1.1.1.

The repository README says the skill includes composition and motion guidance, a kit, examples, and tools that film the result. stageshow/LICENSE is MIT, copyright 2026 Benji Taylor. name: Rune
tagline: Pre-release native GPU Rust UI framework with headless rendering for agents
description:
Rune is a native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework. The README says it targets macOS, Windows, Linux, and the web, with its own renderer, text, layout, and springs. It says every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree, and drive it with scripted input. It ships rune-kit components and tells you to depend on a pinned rev of the dev branch because Rune is pre-release and dev is never rewritten.

The crate split in crates/rune-kit/README.md puts elements and the renderer in crates/rune, and themed components in crates/rune-kit. The root README's license line is "MIT, © Anomaly." The LICENSE file is MIT, copyright 2026 Anomaly. GitHub API on 2026-11-12 reported the MIT license, 6,823 stars, and a push the same day. The catalog's only Rust framework value is rust-gpui, and Rune is not GPUI, so the framework facet is unknown.
agent_guidance:
Pin a rev of dev. The README says Rune is pre-release and that dev is never rewritten. Start from examples/hello and check work by rendering PNGs and reading the element tree, which the README says every app can do headless.

Do not file it as GPUI. rust-gpui is a different framework. The component crate is rune-kit. The README says the project does not take pull requests.
why_it_matters: It is a Rust UI framework that can render headless, so an agent can see the screen it built without a window.
tier_reason: MIT, a clear README, and a push on 2026-11-12. The project says it is pre-release, and the component list was not enumerated on the root README.
notable_for: GPU renderer, text, layout, and springs
macOS, Windows, Linux, and the web

name: Vitrum
tagline: Browser tool that turns a logo into a glass, metal, or colour 3D icon
description:
Vitrum turns a logo into a 3D icon in the browser. The meta description says to turn an SVG or PNG logo into a 3D icon in glass, metal, or colour, and to export a PNG, a GLB for three.js, or an STL for print. It also says the tool is free, in the browser, with no sign-up. The page adds JPG and WebP as inputs. The PNG export is described as the view you set, at 2x, on a transparent background. The GLB is a glTF binary with physically based materials, sized in metres, for three.js, React Three Fiber, and Spline. The STL is a closed mesh in millimetres.

The FAQ says tracing, modelling, and rendering run in the browser, nothing is uploaded, and there is no account. It says everything you export is yours to use, and that you should only upload artwork you own. A license for the Vitrum tool itself was not stated. The page says it is made by Volkan.
pricing_detail: The meta description says "Free, in your browser, no sign-up." No paid plan was on the page.
agent_guidance:
Send a person to https://usevitrum.com with an SVG, PNG, JPG, or WebP they own. The page says the work stays in the browser. Exports are PNG at 2x with a transparent background, GLB for three.js or React Three Fiber, and STL for print.

The FAQ says the export is yours to use. It does not state a license for the Vitrum application. There is no API or install command on the page, so an agent cannot run the conversion itself.
why_it_matters: It makes a 3D icon from a logo in the browser, with PNG, GLB, and STL export, and no account.
tier_reason: The inputs, the three export formats, the local processing, and the free no-account claim are on the page. The tool's own license is not stated.
notable_for: SVG, PNG, JPG, and WebP in
runs in the browser, nothing uploaded

name: unslop
tagline: CC BY skill that restyles AI-looking UI, by Damir Sokolovsky
description:
unslop is an agent skill by Damir Sokolovsky. The README says it turns vibecoded, AI-looking UI into a designed interface, and that it works with Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity. It says the skill finds purple gradients, glows, emoji labels, shouty copy, and uneven spacing, then sets a direction from the product and edits pass by pass. It says it works on whatever the screen is built with, including Next.js, React, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind, or plain HTML and CSS, on dashboards, apps, and landing pages, and on a live site when you only have a link.

Install is a copy into the agent's skills folder, or the Codex skill-installer URL in the README. Story videos need Playwright and ffmpeg. The license section says CC BY 4.0, including commercial use, with credit to Damir Sokolovsky and a link back to the repository. GitHub API on 2026-11-12 reported CC-BY-4.0, 14,909 stars, and a push on 2026-11-08. A separate paid offer, one screen in 3 days, is linked at heydamir.design/unslop. That price was not opened.
pricing_detail: The skill is free under CC BY 4.0. The README links a paid design offer at heydamir.design/unslop and says one key screen takes 3 days. That page was not opened, so no price is recorded here.
agent_guidance:
Copy skills/unslop into the agent's skills folder. The README gives paths for Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity, and a Codex installer command. In Claude Code the command is /unslop. The README says it audits and proposes a direction before it edits.

Credit Damir Sokolovsky and link to https://github.com/heydamir/unslop. The license is CC BY 4.0. Do not treat the skill as tied to one framework. The README says it works on the stack the screen already uses. Image generation through fal, Replicate, OpenAI, or Higgsfield is optional, and the README says it asks before a paid generation.
why_it_matters: It is a widely starred skill whose job is to remove the usual signs of generated UI and restyle the screen that is already there.
tier_reason: CC BY 4.0, a specific install, and 14,909 stars on 2026-11-12. The paid design service's price was not opened.
notable_for: Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity

name: Blueprint
tagline: Describe a generative design tool and Blueprint builds it, with presets and export
description:
Blueprint builds generative design tools from a description. The homepage says to describe a halftone generator, a dither tool, or another generative design tool, and that the result has presets, high-resolution export, and a link for clients. The free plan is 20 credits, described as 10 plus a 10-credit launch bonus, with no card. It covers 3 tools in one project, PNG and SVG export, and no publishing or client sharing. A message costs 3 credits, and Best costs 10. Fixes, use, and export are free.

Paid plans, in US dollars, are Solo at $19 a month or $190 a year, Studio at $49 a month or $490 a year, and Agency at $139 a month or $1,390 a year. A launch offer takes 30 percent off the first month. Yearly billing is described as two months free. Solo includes 300 credits a month, 4 projects, and 1 MCP connection. Studio includes 800 credits, unlimited projects, 1 custom domain, and 3 connections. Agency includes 2,300 credits, 5 custom domains, and 10 connections. The page says MCP uses no credits and is for Solo, Studio, and Agency. The connector URL is https://blueprint.page/api/mcp. Extra packs are 50 credits for $7, 100 for $12, 500 for $49, 1,000 for $89, and 5,000 for $399. The FAQ says you own your prompts, images, tools, and exports. A license for the Blueprint application was not stated. The slug blueprint is already used by another record.
pricing_detail: Free: 20 credits once, 3 tools, 1 project, PNG and SVG, no card. Solo $19/month or $190/year, 300 credits a month. Studio $49/month or $490/year, 800 credits. Agency $139/month or $1,390/year, 2,300 credits. Launch offer: 30 percent off the first month. Extra credit packs from $7 to $399. MCP is on the paid plans and uses no credits.
agent_guidance:
Use the free 20 credits when the user only needs to try a generator and export PNG or SVG. Publishing, client sharing, and the MCP server are on Solo, Studio, or Agency. The page says to add https://blueprint.page/api/mcp as a Claude connector, or to create a token in Settings for Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor.

The FAQ says the user owns the prompts, images, tools, and exports. It does not state a license for Blueprint itself. This record is blueprint-page. The slug blueprint already belongs to a different design-system generator.
why_it_matters: It turns a short description into a working generative design tool, with presets, export, and an MCP connection on the paid plans.
